Field surveys across the southeastern United States indicate that White catfish (Ameiurus catus) attain an ultimate total length of 95 cm [Li = 95 cm], placing them among the larger-bodied members of the Ictaluridae. This maximum recorded length, derived from extensive sampling of lentic populations, is attained by individuals in slow-moving rivers and reservoirs where prey resources are abundant. The growth trajectories of these fish are strongly influenced by thermal regimes, as metabolic rates in this species are temperature-dependent. In controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the age at hatching following egg fertilisation is approximately 11 days [ab = approximately 11 days], a developmental duration that aligns with values reported for congeneric species such as Ameiurus nebulosus. The incubation period is characterised by the progressive absorption of yolk nutrients within the chorionate embryo, leading to the emergence of a yolk-sac larva. At the time of eclosion, the wet weight at birth of these prolarvae is approximately 0.0092 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0092 grams], a modest initial mass derived from an egg diameter of about 2.6 mm that reflects the limited maternal investment per offspring typical of iteroparous ictalurids. This small body mass at emergence necessitates a rapid transition to exogenous feeding to sustain early growth.

Reproductive investment in Ameiurus catus is characterised by a maximum annual fecundity of 3,500 eggs per year [Ri = 3,500 eggs per year] for a gravid female measuring approximately 40 cm in total length and maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This value, equivalent to roughly 10 eggs per day, reflects the species' capacity for high annual reproductive output. The attainment of sexual maturity, marking the onset of gametogenesis and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, occurs at a total length of approximately 45 cm [Lp = approximately 45 cm]. This length at puberty, based on comparative data from Ameiurus melas, indicates that individuals invest considerable somatic growth before reproductive activation. The transition from a post-metamorphic juvenile to a reproductively viable adult involves substantial allometric shifts in body plan, with the onset of vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males triggered by seasonal temperature cues and photoperiod.

Asymptotic body mass is a key life-history parameter for Ameiurus catus, with the ultimate wet weight reaching 10,000 grams [Wwi = 10,000 grams] in the largest individuals. This maximum adult body mass, estimated from length-weight regressions based on the species' ultimate total length, represents a substantial energetic investment in somatic tissue that supports both foraging efficiency and reproductive output. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a typical ictalurid allometry, with individuals exhibiting robust body condition in productive habitats. Under the thermal conditions characteristic of the species' native range, maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] in laboratory settings, the maximum lifespan recorded for Ameiurus catus reaches 5,110 days [am = 5,110 days], a longevity that equates to approximately 14 years. This extended lifespan, documented in both wild populations and captive individuals, allows for multiple reproductive events across the adult life stage, consistent with an iteroparous life-history strategy. Older, senescent adults gradually exhibit reduced condition factors and diminished gonadal recrudescence, leading to eventual physiological death from age-related deterioration of organ function.

The ecological context of White catfish life history reveals a species well adapted to warm, slow-moving freshwater systems. At the experimentally standardised temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the period between successive spawning events is consistent with a rate of approximately 3,500 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 3,500 eggs per year] for a female of about 40 cm total length. This maximum reproductive rate underscores the species' capacity for rapid population turnover in environments where nesting substrate and food resources are abundant. Brood success is strongly dependent on parental nest-guarding behaviour, with males aggressively defending the fertilised eggs against predators. The pelagic larval phase following yolk-sac resorption is brief, as post-metamorphic juveniles quickly adopt a benthic habit. Comparative analyses with other North American ictalurids suggest that the growth efficiency and reproductive scheduling of Ameiurus catus are optimised for seasonal floodplain habitats, where elevated water temperatures and increased prey availability coincide with the species' peak spawning period in late spring and early summer. Dietary studies indicate an ontogenetic shift from zooplankton to benthic macroinvertebrates and small fish as juveniles mature.

Phenotypic variation in growth and reproduction among populations of Ameiurus catus is linked to latitudinal gradients in thermal regime and productivity. In northern parts of its introduced range, individuals may reach a total length at puberty of 45 cm [Lp = 45 cm] only after several additional growing seasons compared to southern conspecifics, reflecting the influence of cooler annual temperatures on metabolic rates. The ultimate total length of 95 cm [Li = 95 cm] appears relatively invariant across populations, suggesting a genetic ceiling on maximum body size that is approached only under optimal conditions. Wet weight at birth remains consistently near 0.0092 grams [Wwb = 0.0092 grams] irrespective of maternal size, indicating that egg diameter is canalised in this species. The age at hatching of 11 days [ab = 11 days] at 25 °C can extend to nearly three weeks in cooler waters, demonstrating the pronounced temperature sensitivity of early ontogeny at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. An ultimate wet weight of 10,000 grams [Wwi = 10,000 grams] and a maximum lifespan of 5,110 days [am = 5,110 days] at 25 °C position Ameiurus catus as a moderately long-lived, fecund species within its guild, occupying an ecological niche that balances relatively rapid juvenile growth with sustained adult reproduction across multiple seasons at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C].
